topic: AI era work philosophy: smart work over hard work
headline_marked: [[AI era winners choose problems, not just work more]], focusing on judgment over sheer output
headline: AI era winners choose problems, not just work more, focusing on judgment over sheer output
summary: In the AI era, success shifts from sheer output to strategic judgment. It's about choosing valuable problems and directing intelligence effectively, rather than simply doing more work.
details: The traditional focus on motivation, discipline, consistency, or obsession as keys to success is shifting. These are merely execution engines; their effectiveness depends entirely on being directed towards worthwhile goals. The real differentiator is "judgment" – the ability to choose what is truly worth pursuing.

Previously, building things was expensive and slow. Now, with AI, the cost of creation has dramatically decreased. This shifts the value from the act of making to the critical tasks of selecting the right problems, understanding their context, and rigorously validating solutions against real-world needs.

The role of an engineer is evolving. Instead of excelling by building faster than others, the advantage now lies in directing intelligence towards the correct problems. Future engineers will function more like architects, researchers, product thinkers, and system designers, focusing on deciding which lines of code are truly valuable.

AI can expand perspectives, simulate stakeholders, and accelerate discovery by generating hypotheses. However, it has limitations; AI cannot fully grasp organizational politics, resistance to change, human habits, or emotional factors present in reality. AI serves as a hypothesis engine, while reality remains the ultimate truth engine.

The journey in tech is no longer a linear path to completion, but a continuous cycle of learning and adaptation. Building enduring capabilities – such as problem identification, systemic thinking, rapid tool adoption, decision-making, and creating tangible value – becomes more crucial than accumulating a static body of knowledge.

topic: HackerRank open sources ATS, resume scoring drama
headline_marked: [[HackerRank open sourced its ATS]]. My resume scored 90/100. Oh wait 74. No – 88
headline: HackerRank open sourced its ATS. My resume scored 90/100. Oh wait 74. No – 88
summary: HackerRank's Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is now open source, allowing developers to test their resumes against the same scoring logic used by recruiters. Initial tests show varied results, highlighting the system's dynamic evaluation.
details: HackerRank has made its Applicant Tracking System (ATS) available as open-source software. This strategic move aims to increase transparency in the hiring process by allowing developers and job seekers to directly examine the algorithms used to evaluate resumes.

The open-sourced ATS includes the core logic for parsing resumes, extracting keywords, and assigning a relevance score. Users can now run their own resumes through the system to understand how they might be perceived by automated screening tools before applying for jobs.

Early community tests have shown fluctuating scores for the same resume, as indicated by the headline's '90/100, Oh wait 74, No – 88' example. This suggests the system's evaluation can be dynamic or sensitive to minor changes and external factors, prompting further exploration by users.

This initiative could empower job seekers to optimize their resumes more effectively by gaining insight into the underlying scoring mechanisms. It also provides a valuable resource for developers interested in building or improving their own recruitment tools and understanding ATS functionality.
